_decision: railButton = 38px / railIcon = 20px. Approved: match the origin Rail Sidebar rail button container at 38px. The 38 below comes from that decision record, not from measuring the component and writing down what it happened to say.
_scope: Anchored to the FIRST pinned rail button only, because an anchor must resolve to exactly one element. This proves the representative instance, not all 27 rail buttons. See sandbox/src/lib/divergence-anchors.tsx.
_history: This value regressed once already and shipped: `size="icon"` carries Button's own `size-9` (36px), and an `h-[38px] w-[38px]` override did NOT win, because tailwind-merge only dedupes within a conflict group and `size-*` vs `h-*`/`w-*` are separate groups. The button rendered 36px while the className read 38. That is precisely the class of regression this check exists to catch mechanically rather than by eye.

checks._width_is_parent_imposed: Named by the audit, kept because 38x38 is the decision: `width: 38` is imposed by the parent flex column (F-1's 54 minus 16 of padding), not by this button's own recipe. Measured directly — strip `size-[38px]` from the live element and width stays 38 while height drops to 20. Only `height` tests this row's own subject; a pass on width means the parent holds, which F-1 asserts separately.

checks._replaces: REPLACED a `box` check that asserted 38x38 at hover. Measured: the button is 38x38 at rest AND at hover, so that assertion passed identically whether hover worked or not — it could not distinguish the state it named. That is checklist item 3's exact failure shape, sitting inside a spec written to enforce item 3.
checks._why: The property hover actually moves is the background. This is the regression M-12 recorded: the button carried `hover:bg-transparent`, suppressing Button's own ghost hover without substituting the dark-rail token, so the rail had NO hover feedback while every box measurement stayed correct. A box check could never have caught it. This one does.
checks._overlap: Deliberately the same assertion as B-2, on a different button. B-2 owns the token decision; this owns 'F-2's representative button still responds to hover at all'. If they ever disagree, one of the two buttons has drifted from the other — which is worth knowing and neither check alone would show.
